Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: The afternoon sun had just reached its peak at the commercial job site when Kai noticed the heavy steel door behind the supply shed swing shut with a metallic bang. It was exactly two o’clock. In that instant, a figure lunged from the shadows, grabbing Kai’s shoulder and pinning him against the concrete wall. The assault was quick, violent, and disorienting, leaving Kai with nothing but a few frozen images burned into his mind: the glint of the attacker’s watch, the scuff of rubber soles on gravel, the cold weight of a hand on his collar. Weeks bled into months, and Kai found himself trapped in a cycle he couldn’t name. Every time the clock on his truck dashboard clicked over to two, the familiar clang of a job-site door, or the sudden sense that he was drifting detached from his own body, he felt a flash of pure dread. Those same sensory cues would yank those fragmented pictures back into his head, but they felt wrong, like a photograph missing half its frame. The pieces wouldn’t connect, and the silence where the rest of the story should be only made him doubt what had actually happened. Instead of finding clarity, the gaps drove him straight to the dashboard drawer where he kept his phone, or to the passenger seat where a flask sat waiting. Each time he scrolled through games or poured a drink to quiet the rising panic, the avoidance only confirmed his own harsh judgments. He told himself he had only gotten into that alley because he was careless, because there was something fundamentally weak in his character that drew danger. That belief that he was inherently flawed didn’t just sit in his head; it poured directly into his nervous system. Every time the thought that he was at fault or that he had no future ahead of him crossed his mind, his shoulders hunched, and his body braced as if danger were already in the room. The self-reproach also deepened the memory fog. When he tried to look back at those frozen moments, the guilt was so intense it blurred the edges, making the snapshots feel heavier and more inescapable. Because he felt the narrative was fundamentally broken, the afternoon hours and the sound of latching doors stopped feeling like neutral events. They became proof of his failure, magnifying every twinge of dread. The incomplete picture felt like a threat still looming, which is why even a coworker’s sudden reach to hand him a tape measure sent him jumping as if struck, his heart hammering against his ribs. To escape the mounting pressure, Kai stopped watching any news or crime dramas, knowing any depiction of violence would spike his alarm. But the withdrawal only tightened the vise. Spending long hours on his phone or nursing a drink to numb the guilt meant he never let his nervous system settle. Each time the screen went dark or the alcohol wore off, the emptiness only made him feel worse about himself, confirming his belief that he was broken and hopeless. The lack of processing kept him permanently primed; an unexpected shift of a colleague’s hand on his shoulder or a loud bang from a power tool would still trigger a full alarm response. And because he relied on those escapes instead of facing the fear, the time of day and the sound of opening doors remained sharp, completely unneutralized. The strategy was eroding his work. As an electrician, Kai’s days required walking unfamiliar job sites, climbing ladders, and navigating spaces where he could never fully map the exits. His avoidance of unknown locations meant he spent more time in the back of supply trucks than on actual runs, and his constant startle response made him miss critical safety checks. He began taking notes on his phone to remember what he was doing, but the habit only reminded him of how detached he felt. On the jobsite, the fear meant he stopped volunteering for after-hours calls, and his foreman noticed the hesitation before Kai even cut power to a live panel. The consequences bled into his personal life, too; his partner’s attempts to check on him felt like invasions, and the silence he cultivated at home only widened the distance between them. Now, sitting in a quiet clinic office, Kai finally admitted he couldn’t outrun the flash of the supply shed door or the weight of the guilt. He was terrified that he would never feel safe in his own skin again, but he was hoping, for the first time in years, that someone might help him piece the picture back together.
